blocks.text: 1. Retraining Strategies

blocks.alt: A trigger leads to retraining, producing a new model version

blocks.text: Drift Detection, the previous topic, closed by pointing directly here for the case of confirmed concept drift. Retraining Strategies define how, and how often, a deployed model actually gets updated once it needs to change.

Retraining is not a one-time event that happens only when a model is first built, it is an ongoing, planned part of running any genuinely real production model over time. This topic closes out the practical, operational half of the Model Deployment module, the part concerned with keeping a live model healthy well after its initial launch.
2. What Triggers a Retraining Run

Scheduled retraining runs on a fixed cadence, every week for instance, regardless of whether any actual drift has been detected in the meantime. Triggered retraining instead fires specifically when Drift Detection or Monitoring, both covered in their own topics, flags a genuine, confirmed problem.

Manual retraining happens when a team makes a deliberate decision to retrain, after a known, major change to the business itself, a new product line launching for instance, that the team already knows will meaningfully change the data's underlying patterns before any automated system would even detect it.

blocks.text: 3. Scheduled Versus Triggered Retraining

blocks.alt: Scheduled retraining runs on a fixed interval while triggered retraining runs on a drift signal

blocks.text: Scheduled retraining is simple and predictable, but it can retrain a model even when nothing has actually meaningfully changed, wasting compute on unnecessary retraining runs that produce essentially the same model as before.

Triggered retraining is considerably more efficient, retraining only when genuinely needed, but it requires reliable Drift Detection already working correctly first, since a triggered strategy is only ever as good as the detection mechanism deciding when to fire it. A broken or overly loose drift detector can leave a triggered strategy silently under-retraining for far too long.
4. What Data Actually Goes Into Retraining

Retraining from scratch on all historical data plus newly collected data is the simplest approach, though it can become genuinely slow as a dataset grows larger and larger over successive retraining cycles. A rolling window approach, using only the most recent 12 months of data for instance, keeps the training set bounded and retraining faster, though it deliberately lets older patterns get forgotten over time.

Fine-tuning an existing model using only new data is the fastest approach of the three, but it carries a real risk of the model drifting away from older, still-valid patterns it once knew well, a risk covered in more depth later in this topic under catastrophic forgetting.
5. Validating Before Deploying

blocks.alt: A new model gets validated before deploy, then deployed

blocks.text: This connects directly back to Cross Validation and the full suite of Model Evaluation modules covered earlier in this course. A newly retrained model must be validated exactly as rigorously as the original model was when it was first built, never simply assumed to be an improvement just because it is newer.

The new model's metrics get compared directly against the currently deployed model's metrics on the same evaluation criteria. If the new model genuinely outperforms the current one, deployment can proceed; if it does not, the retrained model should not be deployed at all, and the team should instead investigate why retraining failed to actually help.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A surprisingly common mistake is deploying every retrained model automatically without this comparison step, on the assumption that newer data always means a better model. Retraining can sometimes make a model worse, due to a bad data batch or a genuine labeling error, and validation is what catches this before it reaches production.

blocks.text: 6. The Champion-Challenger Pattern

blocks.alt: A champion, the current model, is compared against a challenger, the new model

blocks.text: The champion-challenger pattern names the currently deployed production model the champion, and the newly retrained model the challenger. Both get run side by side, either on live traffic split between them, or on a held-out, genuinely recent dataset neither model was trained on.

The challenger only gets promoted to replace the champion if it genuinely, measurably wins on the agreed comparison metrics, a disciplined, structured way of applying the validation step covered in the previous section in an ongoing, repeatable fashion across every future retraining cycle.
7. The Rollback Plan

blocks.alt: A new model that underperforms triggers a rollback to the previous version

blocks.text: This connects back to the version-tracking concern raised throughout the Serialization topic and the Model Deployment module more broadly. Every retrained model gets deployed as a new, distinct version, never simply overwriting the previous one in place.

If a newly deployed model underperforms once it is genuinely live, serving real traffic, the team can roll back instantly to the previous, known-good version rather than being stuck with a worse model while a fix gets developed. A rollback plan is not an optional extra, it is the direct, essential safety net underneath every single retraining decision a team makes.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This is precisely why the Model Registry topic, covered in the upcoming Production Machine Learning module, matters so directly here: a well-organized registry of versioned models is what makes a fast, confident rollback actually possible in practice.

blocks.text: 8. A Genuine Risk: Catastrophic Forgetting

blocks.alt: Retraining on new data only can forget old patterns

blocks.text: A genuine risk specific to fine-tuning-style retraining on new data only, already flagged earlier in this topic, is that the model can forget older, still-valid patterns while learning from newer data, a phenomenon called catastrophic forgetting.

This risk is mitigated by periodically retraining from a fuller, more complete historical dataset instead of fine-tuning indefinitely on new data alone, ensuring the model periodically re-anchors itself against the full breadth of patterns it originally needed to learn, not just whatever happened to arrive most recently.

blocks.text: 9. Choosing a Retraining Strategy in Practice

A stable domain experiencing only slow, gradual data drift is often well served by scheduled retraining, monthly for instance, without needing the added complexity of a fully triggered system. A fast-changing domain, fraud detection for instance, benefits far more from triggered retraining, reacting quickly to genuine, sudden shifts rather than waiting for the next fixed schedule point.

A known, major upcoming business change calls for manual retraining, planned deliberately ahead of the change itself, so the model is ready with fresh, relevant data the moment that change actually takes effect, rather than reacting to it only after the fact.
10. Worked Example
The example below implements a simple champion-challenger comparison, retraining a challenger model and only promoting it if it genuinely beats the current champion.

code.content:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
import numpy as np
import joblib

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X_old = rng.normal(size=(2000, 5))
y_old = (X_old[:, 0] + X_old[:, 2] > 0).astype(int)
X_new = rng.normal(size=(500, 5))
y_new = (X_new[:, 0] + X_new[:, 2] - 0.3 * X_new[:, 4] > 0).astype(int)  # slightly shifted relationship

X_combined = np.vstack([X_old, X_new])
y_combined = np.concatenate([y_old, y_new])
X_train, X_holdout, y_train, y_holdout = train_test_split(X_combined, y_combined, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

champion = joblib.load("model_v1.joblib") if False else RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42).fit(X_old, y_old)
challenger = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)
challenger.fit(X_train, y_train)

champion_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_holdout, champion.predict(X_holdout))
challenger_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_holdout, challenger.predict(X_holdout))

print(f"Champion accuracy on holdout: {champion_accuracy:.4f}")
print(f"Challenger accuracy on holdout: {challenger_accuracy:.4f}")

if challenger_accuracy > champion_accuracy:
    joblib.dump(challenger, "model_v2.joblib")
    print("Challenger wins: promoted to model_v2.joblib, champion retained as fallback for rollback")
else:
    print("Challenger did not beat the champion: not deployed, investigate the retraining data")

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Notice the champion model is deliberately retained even after a successful promotion, exactly the rollback safety net covered earlier in this topic, ready to be restored instantly if the newly promoted challenger underperforms once live.

blocks.text: 11. Model Deployment: Key Takeaways

items: Retraining is an ongoing, planned part of running any real production model, not a one-time event.
Retraining can be triggered on a schedule, by a detected drift signal, or manually by a team's deliberate decision.
Scheduled retraining is simple but can waste compute; triggered retraining is efficient but depends on reliable drift detection.
Retraining data can be full history plus new data, a bounded rolling window, or new-data-only fine-tuning, each with real tradeoffs.
A newly retrained model must be validated with the same rigor as the original, never assumed to be better simply because it is newer.
The champion-challenger pattern promotes a retrained model only if it genuinely, measurably beats the current one.
Every retrained model deploys as a new version, enabling an instant rollback if it underperforms once live.
Fine-tuning on new data only risks catastrophic forgetting of older patterns, mitigated by periodic full retraining.
